t: IndiaAI Mission: seven pillars, Rs 10,372 crore outlay and the national AI stack
b: The IndiaAI Mission was launched in March 2024 with an outlay of Rs 10,372 crore to build an end-to-end sovereign AI ecosystem. It is organised around seven pillars: compute capacity, foundation models, datasets through the AIKosh platform, AI applications, FutureSkills talent programmes, safe and trusted AI, and startup financing. Within roughly two years the mission onboarded more than 38 thousand GPUs for a common compute facility offered to Indian startups and academia at subsidised rates, shortlisted twelve organisations to build indigenous large and small language models, approved thirty India-specific AI applications, established twenty seven India Data and AI labs with 543 more identified, and began supporting thousands of students from undergraduate to PhD level. The design principle is a shared national compute pool rather than duplicated captive capacity.

t: IndiaAI compute capacity: 38,231 GPUs from 14 empanelled providers at about Rs 65 per GPU hour
b: As on March 2026 the IndiaAI Mission had onboarded 38,231 GPUs from 14 empanelled AI service providers under the IndiaAI Compute Capacity framework. Eligible users include startups, MSMEs, researchers, academic institutions, students and government entities, who request capacity through the IndiaAI Compute Portal. The average subsidised rate is approximately Rs 65 per GPU per hour, with select high-end GPUs priced higher. Empanelled providers supply storage, networking and AI platform services alongside raw compute. Data centres hosting the capacity are distributed across Mumbai, Navi Mumbai, Hyderabad, Bengaluru, Noida and Jamnagar. A further 20,000 GPUs are in the process of being added. The subsidy model is deliberate: it lowers the entry cost of training and inference for Indian builders instead of subsidising foreign cloud spend.

t: Sarvam-105B model card: 105B parameter MoE, 128K context, Apache 2.0, Indian language native
b: Sarvam-105B is a flagship chat model with a mixture-of-experts architecture and 128 sparse experts using multi-head latent attention, pre-trained on 12 trillion tokens and released under Apache 2.0. It supports a 128,000 token context window and is exposed through an OpenAI-compatible chat completions endpoint. A conversational sibling, sarvam-105b-conversations, is post-trained for real-time dialogue and voice agents with a 32,000 token window. The model targets the ten most spoken Indian languages plus English, accepting native script, romanised and code-mixed input. Its positioning is complex reasoning, code generation, long-context document analysis and agentic tool use. The earlier Sarvam-M 24B model has been deprecated in favour of the 105B line. Pricing is quoted in rupees per million tokens, which keeps cost accounting in the domestic currency.

t: Sarvam-30B and Sarvam-105B unveiled at the India AI Impact Summit 2026, trained entirely in India
b: At the India AI Impact Summit 2026 in Hyderabad, Sarvam AI released Sarvam-30B and Sarvam-105B, both trained in India. The 30B model uses a mixture-of-experts design pre-trained on 16 trillion tokens with a 32,000 token context window and one billion activated parameters, aimed at low-latency conversational workloads, and is benchmarked against open models of similar size. The 105B model carries nine billion active parameters and a 128,000 token context window for long-form reasoning, coding and Indian language processing. BharatGen used the same event to unveil Param2, a 17B mixture-of-experts model built on an NVIDIA training stack and optimised for Indic languages across governance, education, healthcare and agriculture. BharatGen stated that its models and tooling would be open-sourced on Hugging Face.

t: BharatGen Param2 17B MoE: India's flagship sovereign multilingual model from the IIT Bombay consortium
b: BharatGen is an IIT Bombay led consortium supported under the IndiaAI foundation model pillar to build multilingual and multimodal models ranging from 2 billion to 1 trillion parameters on an open-source basis. Its Param2 model is a 17 billion parameter mixture-of-experts system optimised for multiple Indic languages and aimed at governance, education, healthcare, agriculture and enterprise use. The government describes BharatGen as having developed the Param2 model with a strong Indic benchmark showing, and both BharatGen and Sarvam models are now listed on the AIKosh platform so that other startups and researchers can build on them. The consortium's stated intent is to keep models and tooling open rather than gated, so that Indian language capability is not rented from abroad.

t: Twelve organisations selected to build India's foundation models: the full cohort
b: Under the IndiaAI Innovation Centre foundation models pillar, twelve organisations and consortia were selected from 506 proposals. They are Sarvam AI building an open-source 120 billion parameter model for governance use cases; Soket AI with a 120 billion parameter multilingual model for defence, healthcare and education; Gnani AI with a 14 billion parameter voice model; Gan AI with a 70 billion parameter multilingual model targeting text to speech; Avataar AI with domain AI avatars up to 70 billion parameters; the IIT Bombay consortium BharatGen spanning 2 billion to 1 trillion parameters; Fractal Analytics with a 70 billion parameter reasoning model; Tech Mahindra Maker's Lab with an 8 billion parameter Indic model and an agentic platform named Orion; Zenteiq with the BrahmAI science model; GenLoop with 2 billion parameter Yukti, Varta and Kavach small models covering all 22 scheduled languages; Intellihealth with a 20 billion parameter EEG model; and Shodh AI with a 7 billion parameter materials discovery model. The models are trained on datasets spanning all 22 scheduled Indian languages.

t: AIKosh: controlled access to India-based datasets and sovereign model tryouts
b: AIKosh is the IndiaAI Mission platform for controlled and secure access to India-based datasets, intended to support data governance, privacy protection and responsible data use. It hosts dataset collections contributed by government departments and research institutions, and provides model tryout pages so developers can test sovereign models before integrating them. Sarvam and BharatGen models were made available on AIKosh for the developer community following their 2026 launch. IndicTrans2, the AI4Bharat translation model for 22 scheduled languages, is published on the platform with a tryout interface. For a search or research product, AIKosh is the sanctioned route to Indian-language training data and to on-platform inference without sending citizen data to foreign clouds.

t: India AI Governance Guidelines: the seven sutras and what they require of a search or AI system
s: Principal Scientific Adviser to the Government of India
b: The India AI Governance Guidelines, drafted by a MeitY committee constituted in July 2025 and released in November 2025, set out seven sutras adapted from the RBI FREE-AI committee report: Trust is the Foundation; People First; Innovation over Restraint; Fairness and Equity; Accountability; Understandable by Design; and Safety, Resilience and Sustainability. The framework is principle-based and technology neutral, recommends building on existing laws rather than a new statute, and proposes institutions including an AI Governance Group, a Technology and Policy Expert Committee and an AI Safety Institute. For builders, the operative requirements are disclosure of how a system reaches an answer, visible accountability for outputs, avoidance of bias against marginalised groups, human oversight in sensitive domains, and preference for lightweight resource-efficient models.

t: AI Safety Institute, AI Governance Group and Technology and Policy Expert Committee explained
b: The India AI Governance Guidelines recommend three new national institutions. The AI Governance Group provides strategic coordination across ministries; the Technology and Policy Expert Committee supplies expert advisory input; and the AI Safety Institute carries out technical validation and safety research, including testing for deepfake detection and content provenance. The guidelines also recommend an India-specific AI risk assessment and classification framework focused on vulnerable groups, a national federated AI incident reporting mechanism, proportionate voluntary risk mitigation through standards and audits, and mandatory human oversight in sensitive and critical sectors. Existing bodies retain enforcement roles, including CERT-In for cyber incidents, the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre, the National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre and the Data Protection Board under the DPDP Act.

t: Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023: consent, purpose limitation and what it means for indexing
b: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 governs the collection and processing of digital personal data in India. It requires consent or a specified legitimate use for processing, limits use to the stated purpose, mandates data minimisation and accuracy, and creates obligations for data fiduciaries including security safeguards and breach notification. Significant data fiduciaries carry additional duties such as impact assessment and appointment of a data protection officer. The Act establishes the Data Protection Board of India as the enforcement body. For any search or retrieval product the practical consequences are: do not index personal data without a lawful basis, honour erasure requests, keep processing local where possible, and disclose in plain language what is stored. Consent managers under the account aggregator model are the recognised mechanism for user-controlled data sharing.

t: Bhashini at scale: 22 languages by voice, 36 by text, 350+ models, 4 billion inferences
b: Bhashini, the National Language Translation Mission launched in 2022, is India's language layer as digital public infrastructure. It supports voice in 22 languages and text services in 36 languages, hosts more than 350 AI models and datasets, and has completed over 4 billion language inferences. Its stated purpose is to remove three barriers together: the language barrier, the digital interface barrier and the literacy barrier that forces reading and typing. Services include automatic speech recognition, machine translation, text to speech, transliteration, voice cloning and document understanding, delivered as APIs so platforms can add language capability without building models themselves. Deployment examples include real-time speech translation at Kashi Tamil Sangamam and the Kumbh Sah'AI'yak multilingual chatbot at Maha Kumbh 2025, which served pilgrims in 11 languages with navigation, event information and a digital lost and found.

t: Bhashini API catalogue: service IDs for ASR, translation, transliteration, TTS and language detection
b: Bhashini exposes models through REST APIs addressed by service ID. For speech recognition, entries include an AI4Bharat multilingual conformer covering all 22 scheduled languages plus Bhojpuri, Chhattisgarhi, Haryanvi and Bhili through Bodhan.AI, Dravidian language models from IIT Madras, and Hindi conformer models from AI4Bharat. Translation service IDs include IIIT Hyderabad's nmt-all covering 36 languages and Hinglish, AI4Bharat's indictrans-v2-all, IIT Bombay's trilingual English-Hindi-Marathi model, C-DAC Noida and Pune models, and a Sanskrit to Tamil route from IIIT Hyderabad. Transliteration is served by AI4Bharat IndicXlit over 21 languages. Text to speech is served by IIT Madras, AI4Bharat coqui models split by language family, IISc SYSPIN and Bodhan. Language identification is available as indic-lang-detection-all. Each service ID is independently versioned and quota-managed.

t: IndicTrans2: the first open translation model covering all 22 scheduled Indian languages
b: IndicTrans2 is the first open-source transformer-based multilingual machine translation model supporting all 22 scheduled Indian languages, including multiple scripts for low-resource languages such as Kashmiri, Manipuri and Sindhi. It adopts script unification where feasible so that transfer learning can share lexical information across languages, covering Perso-Arabic, Ol Chiki, Meitei, Latin and Devanagari scripts. The work contributed four missing pieces: BPCC, the largest public parallel corpus for Indic languages; IN22, the first n-way parallel benchmark across all 22 languages with India-origin content across thirteen domains; the models themselves; and permissive open licensing for commercial deployment. A distilled variant about one fifth the size provides comparable quality at lower deployment cost, and IndicTrans2-M2M supports 462 direct translation directions between Indian languages.

t: BPCC and IN22: 230 million bitext pairs and an India-origin translation benchmark
b: The Bharat Parallel Corpus Collection contains about 230 million bitext pairs for Indic languages, of which roughly 126 million were newly added, including 644 thousand manually translated sentence pairs created by an in-house team. Seed data covers human translations of English sentences into all 22 Indic languages across multiple domains, and filled gaps for seven languages that previously had no manually created parallel data. IN22 is the accompanying benchmark with an English source-original side, drawn from India-specific articles across culture, economy, education, entertainment, geography, government, health, industry, legal, news, religion, sports and tourism, plus a conversational subset built from everyday Indian context prompts. The corpus and benchmark are released with permissive licences so that downstream products can be evaluated on Indian content rather than translated foreign text.

t: IndicXlit and Aksharantar: roman to native script transliteration for 21 languages
b: IndicXlit is a transformer-based multilingual transliteration model of about 11 million parameters for Roman to native script conversion and back, supporting 21 Indic languages. It is trained on Aksharantar, described as the largest publicly available parallel corpus for this task with 26 million word pairs spanning 20 Indic languages. In a search product transliteration matters more than it appears: Indian users type Hinglish queries such as aadhaar, upi kitna or bhashini kaise, and a retrieval engine that only matches Devanagari or only matches English will silently fail on a large share of real queries. Running queries through IndicXlit before indexing and at query time is the standard fix, and Bhashini exposes it as the ai4bharat/indicxlit--cpu-fsv2 service.

t: Indic speech recognition: conformer and whisper models for 22 languages on commodity hardware
b: IndicConformer is a conformer-based automatic speech recognition model with only about 30 million parameters, built for real-time speech recognition in Indian languages and small enough to deploy on an Android device or serve over websockets. It was trained on ULCA, Kathbath, Shrutilipi and MUCS datasets. A separate IndicWhisper line uses the whisper architecture for higher accuracy at higher compute cost. AI4Bharat states that its speech work was funded through MeitY grants and that it operates as the Data Management Unit of Bhashini, gathering transcribed audio from over 400 districts across all 22 scheduled languages. For a voice-first search interface the conformer class is the practical choice: latency stays low, the model runs on-device, and no audio leaves the phone.

t: Indic text to speech: FastPitch acoustic models with HiFi-GAN vocoders for Indian voices
b: Indic-TTS is ongoing research on multispeaker text to speech for Indian languages, split into two models: an acoustic model that generates a waveform representation for given text, and a vocoder that synthesises audio from it. The released pipeline uses FastPitch for acoustics and HiFi-GAN for vocoding. Bhashini serves these through service IDs split by language family, with AI4Bharat coqui models covering Dravidian and Indo-Aryan groups, IIT Madras covering 23 languages, IISc SYSPIN covering Kannada, Telugu, English, Hindi, Marathi, Bengali, Gujarati, Maithili, Bhojpuri, Chhattisgarhi and Magahi, and Bodhan covering the full scheduled list. For a search engine, TTS is the accessibility layer: results read aloud in the user's language, which matters for low-literacy users and for hands-free use.

t: Airavata, IndicBERT and Sangraha: the open Indic language model family
b: AI4Bharat, a research lab at IIT Madras, develops open datasets, tools and models for Indian languages across transliteration, natural language understanding, generation, translation, speech recognition and speech synthesis. Its language models include IndicBERT for understanding tasks, IndicBART for generation and Airavata for instruction following, trained on corpora such as IndicCorpora and Sangraha. The lab states that its work is deployed in real-world use cases across academia, industry and government, and that it holds grants from MeitY while running the data management unit of Bhashini. For a retrieval system the most useful artefact is the embedding side: IndicBERT-class encoders give dense vectors that behave sensibly on Indian-language text where an English-only sentence encoder collapses distinct queries into one neighbourhood.

t: Kumbh Sah'AI'yak: a multilingual voice chatbot in 11 languages at Maha Kumbh 2025
b: Bhashini powered the Kumbh Sah'AI'yak chatbot at Maha Kumbh 2025, a multilingual and voice-enabled assistant that gave pilgrims navigation and event information in 11 languages, covering Hindi, English and nine others. It also ran a digital lost and found function with real-time text and voice translation so that families separated at the gathering could be reunited across language barriers. The case is a useful reference point for anyone building a conversational interface for India: the hard requirements were low-bandwidth operation, tolerance of dialect and accent variation, voice input for users who do not type, and answers short enough to be heard once and understood. It demonstrates that a language-first assistant is a service delivery mechanism, not a novelty.

t: Sansad Bhashini: AI translation, transcription and summarisation inside Parliament
b: Sansad Bhashini is the deployment of Bhashini language technology inside Parliament for multilingual translation, transcription and summarisation of proceedings, so that members can follow business in Indian languages. The platform reports over a million mobile app downloads, more than a billion inferences, and a large user base across states. It operates as an ecosystem rather than a single vendor product: research institutions, language experts, startups, state governments and industry partners contribute models, which are then composed into service flows. For a research tool the lesson is architectural: the language layer should be an interchangeable set of service IDs behind a stable interface, so that a better ASR or translation model can be swapped in without rewriting the product.

t: Aadhaar: 144 crore identities and 2,707 crore authentication transactions in one year
b: Aadhaar is the world's largest digital identity programme, providing biometric and demographic based unique identity to residents. As of March 2026 more than 144 crore Aadhaar numbers had been generated, and in 2024-25 alone over 2,707 crore authentication transactions were carried out. Aadhaar e-KYC had processed more than 2,458 crore transactions by late June 2026. The identity layer was seeded through the JAM trinity of Jan Dhan bank accounts, Aadhaar enrolment and mobile penetration, which let welfare benefits move directly into bank accounts and reduced leakage. Identity became portable and verification near instant. For software, Aadhaar is the anchor for consent-based identity assertions: a product does not store the number, it stores a verified claim and a purpose, which is the pattern the DPDP Act expects.

t: UPI in FY 2025-26: 24,161 crore transactions worth Rs 314 lakh crore
b: The Unified Payments Interface processed 24,161.69 crore transactions worth Rs 314.23 lakh crore in FY 2025-26. It serves more than 55.49 crore individuals and 6.5 crore merchants and connects 731 banks on one platform, accounting for about 85 percent of India's digital payment volume and nearly half of global real-time payment transaction volume. Monthly volume grew from 0.01 crore transactions in 2016 to over 2,000 crore by 2025, and the platform handles roughly 66 crore transactions a day. Micro-payments dominate: 86 percent of merchant transactions are below Rs 500. UPI is accepted in 11 foreign countries including Singapore, UAE, France, Mauritius and Cambodia. The IMF recognised it as the world's largest retail fast payment system by volume in its June 2025 report.

t: ONDC by mid 2026: 20 crore buyers, 5 lakh sellers, 1,000 cities, 90 lakh monthly transactions
b: The Open Network for Digital Commerce, launched in 2022, is an open network that connects buyers and sellers through interoperable platforms instead of a single marketplace, so that discovery and fulfilment are separated from any one application. By June 2026 it reported over 20 crore buyers, 5 lakh sellers, presence in 1,000 cities and nearly 90 lakh monthly transactions. Integration with eSaras and Indiahandmade extended market access to self-help groups, weavers and artisans across more than 11 buyer apps, and a Sahayak WhatsApp bot supports small businesses in five languages. ONDC is the clearest Indian example of a protocol-first alternative to platform lock-in, and it is the closest existing model for a search layer that indexes participants rather than owning them.

t: DigiLocker: 72 crore users and over 936 crore documents issued by 2,822 issuers
b: DigiLocker, launched in 2015, is a secure digital document wallet that lets citizens store, access and share authenticated electronic documents with consent-based access. As of mid 2026 it had more than 72 crore registered users, over 936 crore documents issued through 2,822 onboarded issuers, and 5,437 document types available, split between 661 central and 4,776 state services. In a single recent year 17.9 crore users registered and 26.74 crore documents were issued. Because documents originate with the issuer rather than being uploaded by the citizen, verification is against the source of truth and forged documents are structurally harder. Platforms are hosted in government data centres with SSL, Aadhaar or OTP based authentication, Parichay-based access control, encryption, VAPT and CERT-In aligned security audits.

t: UMANG: 2,575 government services from 241 departments in one application
b: UMANG, the Unified Mobile Application for New-age Governance launched in 2017, provides a single window on mobile and web for central, state and local government services. As on 31 July 2026 it offered approximately 2,575 services, 880 from central government and 1,695 from states, across 241 departments, and had more than 11.66 crore registered users with about 798 crore transactions over three years. Services span EPFO balances and claims, PAN and Aadhaar services, DigiLocker access, utility payments, pensions, scholarships, passport and driving licence services and exam results. UMANG is integrated with Aadhaar, eSign and API Setu. For a search product, UMANG is the canonical example of a fragmented service catalogue that a good retrieval layer can make navigable.

t: API Setu: 8,904 government APIs published for interoperable service delivery
b: API Setu is the government's API directory, intended to promote efficient sharing of data among data owners and between government agencies so that services can be delivered in an integrated manner. As of July 2026 the portal had published 8,904 APIs contributed by central and state government departments. It sits alongside MeriPehchaan, the national single sign-on, and the core digital public infrastructure components. Practically, API Setu is the discovery layer for a builder: it is where a search or assistant product would look for a sanctioned, rate-limited interface to scheme data, document verification, or service status, rather than scraping portals. Its existence is also an architectural argument: public data is meant to be consumed through published contracts, not crawlers.

t: GeM: Rs 18.4 lakh crore cumulative procurement, with 11 lakh MSMEs selling to government
b: The Government eMarketplace digitises public procurement and widens participation in government contracting. By June 2026 it had recorded over Rs 18.4 lakh crore in cumulative gross merchandise value, including Rs 5 lakh crore in FY 2025-26, and enabled more than 11 lakh MSMEs to access government markets. The platform covers over 10,894 product categories and 348 service categories with more than 1.67 lakh buyer organisations onboard, and over 24 lakh sellers and service providers have completed profiles. Women-led businesses recorded Rs 83,323 crore and startups Rs 54,005.8 crore in cumulative order value under the SWAYATT initiative. As a data source it is unusually structured: every order carries a category, a buyer and a value, which makes procurement a good proving ground for faceted search.

t: Direct Benefit Transfer: over Rs 52 lakh crore moved across 318 schemes and 56 ministries
b: Aadhaar-linked Direct Benefit Transfer moves welfare benefits directly from 318 schemes across 56 ministries into beneficiary bank accounts, and cumulative transfers have crossed Rs 52 lakh crore. The Public Financial Management System provides end-to-end monitoring of government funds and electronic payments, and was mandated for DBT payment, accounting and reporting in December 2014. The government reports savings of more than Rs 4.31 lakh crore between 2015 and March 2024 from removing duplicate and fake beneficiaries. The National Scholarship Portal has disbursed about 8.16 crore scholarships worth roughly Rs 53,300 crore through DBT. The relevant lesson for information systems is that identity plus a payment rail plus a status API turns a paper entitlement into a queryable fact.

t: eSign and e-Hastakshar: 155 crore legally valid electronic signatures issued
b: eSign is an online electronic signature service that can be integrated through an API so that a user can digitally sign a document in a legally acceptable form. A total of 155.56 crore eSigns have been issued by all eSign service providers, of which 44.23 crore were issued by C-DAC under the e-Hastakshar project, with about 12.46 crore issued in the last year. The service is built on Aadhaar-based authentication and is operated by licensed providers under the IT Act framework. For a research or records product this matters because it closes the loop on provenance: a document can be authenticated at issue, hashed at index time, and signed by the party that published it, giving three independent checks rather than one.

t: myScheme: 4,750 government schemes with 385 crore API hits
b: myScheme is a national platform that lets citizens discover and access information on government schemes offered by central and state governments. It hosts over 4,750 schemes and has recorded more than 4.5 crore visitors, 6.5 lakh registered users and over 385 crore API hits. The platform's design problem is the same one a search engine faces at larger scale: eligibility rules are written in administrative language, schemes overlap, names differ between states, and the user knows their situation but not the scheme's name. Any serious Indian search product should treat scheme discovery as a first-class vertical, because it is the highest-value query class for ordinary citizens and the one least served by general web search.

t: Account Aggregator framework: consent-based financial data sharing with purpose limitation
b: The Account Aggregator framework, introduced by the Reserve Bank of India, lets an individual share financial data across institutions through licensed consent managers rather than by handing over credentials. Data flows are purpose-bound, time-bound and revocable, and the consent artefact records who asked, for what, for how long and for which accounts. The model is now applied beyond finance as the reference design for user-controlled data sharing in India. It is the pattern to copy when a product needs personal context for research: ask for a specific slice for a specific purpose, record the grant, and expire it. It is also the mechanism the DPDP Act anticipates when it refers to consent managers, which makes it both a technical and a compliance choice.

t: Vishvasya: MeitY's National Blockchain Framework stack offering Blockchain-as-a-Service
b: MeitY launched the Vishvasya Blockchain Technology Stack on 4 September 2024 to offer Blockchain-as-a-Service on geographically distributed infrastructure for permissioned blockchain applications. The National Blockchain Framework is architected with distributed infrastructure, core framework functionality, smart contracts and an API gateway, plus security, privacy and interoperability layers, and it currently supports two permissioned platforms while remaining extensible. It is hosted in NIC data centres at Bhubaneswar, Pune and Hyderabad. The stack provides a dashboard for automated network setup, a generic smart contract layer, authentication and authorisation functions, open APIs for recording and querying contracts, node management, security-audited containers and hardened docker images. It supports NFT and oracle integrations and an indigenous certification authority with indigenous crypto modules for key storage.

t: NBFLite: the lightweight blockchain sandbox for Indian startups and academia
o: C-DAC / NIC / IDRBT / IIT Hyderabad / IIIT Hyderabad / SETS
b: NBFLite is a lightweight blockchain framework for research, experimentation and rapid prototyping, powered by the National Blockchain Framework. It supports Hyperledger Fabric and Hyperledger Sawtooth in single node setups and bundles smart contract templates for insurance, supply chain, certificates and drug track and trace. It was developed jointly by C-DAC, NIC, IDRBT Hyderabad, IIT Hyderabad, IIIT Hyderabad and SETS Chennai under MeitY support. The purpose is to remove the two barriers that stop Indian teams from building on-chain applications: the cost of standing up a network, and the absence of domain-specific contract templates. For a prototype, NBFLite is the sanctioned starting point; for production, the same contracts move to the Vishvasya BaaS stack without a rewrite.

t: Praamaanik: blockchain-backed verification of mobile app origin
b: Praamaanik is a blockchain-enabled solution for verifying the origin and authenticity of mobile applications. Developers upload an app and its unique details are recorded on the blockchain ledger; citizens then check an app against those records to confirm that it is the genuine build from the claimed publisher, using the M Kavach 2 mobile security application. The problem it addresses is fraudulent and repackaged apps that impersonate legitimate services and harvest credentials, including fake customer support applications. It is the clearest citizen-facing use of the National Blockchain Framework, and it demonstrates the right pattern for provenance systems generally: record the claim at the moment of publication, make verification cheap and public, and let the user check without trusting the verifier.

t: National Blockchain Framework: 34 crore documents verified, Rs 64.76 crore outlay
b: The National Blockchain Framework was initiated in March 2021 with a budget outlay of Rs 64.76 crore and formally launched on 4 September 2024. Its core components are the Vishvasya blockchain stack, NBFLite, Praamaanik and the National Blockchain Portal, deployed across NIC data centres in Bhubaneswar, Pune and Hyderabad. Over 34 crore documents had been verified on the platform as of 21 October 2025. Live applications include property chain for revenue departments in Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Jharkhand; certificate chain for education and revenue records in Karnataka, Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra, Delhi, Manipur and Puducherry; and drug logistics supply chain for the Karnataka State Medical Supplies Corporation. A blockchain-based SMS header registry covering over 1.13 lakh entities was built with RBI, SEBI, NIC and C-DAC.

t: Blockchain for land records and certificates: what Indian states actually run in production
b: Government answers in Parliament list the blockchain applications hosted on National Blockchain Framework infrastructure. Property chain runs for the Revenue Department, Town Municipal Council and City Corporation of Karnataka, the Departments of Revenue and Survey in Andhra Pradesh, and the Department of Revenue in Jharkhand. Certificate chain covers revenue records and economic statistics in Karnataka, Indira Gandhi Krishi Vishwavidyalaya in Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra University of Health Sciences in Nashik, the Revenue Department in Delhi, the Council of Higher Secondary Education in Manipur, the Department of Civil Supplies in Puducherry, and a service level training record system for the Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel National Police Academy. Drug logistics supply chain runs for the Karnataka State Medical Supplies Corporation. These are production systems, not pilots, which matters when judging whether Indian blockchain infrastructure is real.

t: National Strategy on Blockchain: MeitY's roadmap for adoption across governance and industry
b: The National Strategy on Blockchain developed by MeitY sets out a roadmap for blockchain adoption in India, identifies challenges across technology, regulation and skills, and defines short-term and long-term goals for integration across domains. It is the policy parent of the National Blockchain Framework, which turned the strategy into shared infrastructure. The strategy takes a permissioned-first position suited to government record keeping: known participants, auditable governance, and no requirement for public token economics. It also flags the risks it intends to manage, including vendor lock-in, interoperability across divergent platforms, performance and scalability limits, and the shortage of trained developers. NIC's Centre of Excellence in Blockchain Technology supports departments with proof of concept work on Hyperledger Fabric, Sawtooth and Ethereum before scale deployment.

t: BharatNet and rural connectivity: 2.21 lakh gram panchayats on optical fibre
b: BharatNet is the national optical fibre programme extending broadband to gram panchayats, with over 2.21 lakh gram panchayats enabled and more than 5 lakh Common Service Centres functioning as last-mile access points, including 3.91 lakh at panchayat level. Internet subscribers rose from 25.15 crore in 2014 to over 109.2 crore by the end of March 2026, and over 6.39 crore people have been trained in digital literacy. The design implication for a search product is bandwidth realism: a rural user on a shared connection cannot absorb a two megabyte page, so an engine that ships a lean interface and answers in text rather than video will reach more of the country than one that assumes fibre.

t: Bharat 6G Vision: indigenous research, standards and IP by 2030
b: The Bharat 6G Vision aims to position India among global leaders in sixth generation telecom by 2030, with emphasis on indigenous research, intellectual property creation, standards development and next-generation telecom innovation. It sits alongside a wider telecom reform programme covering spectrum, licensing and satellite communication. For software architecture the practical relevance is latency and device assumptions: a 6G era assumes edge inference, always-on connectivity and dense device meshes, which argues for search products that degrade gracefully to offline mode rather than assuming a fat server. It also matters for standards work, because whoever defines the interface between networks and AI services sets terms for everyone else, and India's stated position is that it intends to be a definer rather than only an adopter.

t: NavIC: India's regional satellite navigation system and its use in geospatial services
b: NavIC, the Navigation with Indian Constellation, is India's regional satellite navigation system built and operated by ISRO, providing position, navigation and timing services over India and an extended surrounding region. It is designed to serve both civilian and strategic users and is being mandated in phases for devices and applications in India, including vehicle tracking and public fleet management. For a search product, NavIC matters at the layer above positioning: local relevance. Queries such as nearby hospital, which office handles this, or where is the camp are resolved by joining a place name to an authoritative boundary and service dataset. Owning the positioning layer means the relevance model does not have to rent its geography from a foreign provider.

t: Param Rudra: three indigenous supercomputing systems under the National Supercomputing Mission
b: Under the National Supercomputing Mission, the government commissioned Param Rudra supercomputing systems at three institutions, with C-DAC as the implementing agency and an outlay in the range of Rs 850 crore for the tranche. The systems support weather and climate research, materials science, and other compute-heavy scientific work, and they form part of a wider mission that has deployed tens of petaflops of capacity across academic and research institutions in India. Alongside the IndiaAI Mission GPU cloud, the supercomputing mission is the second leg of domestic compute: one optimised for AI training and inference, the other for simulation and scientific workloads. Together they are the reason a sovereign AI story in India is not purely aspirational.

t: India Semiconductor Mission: fabs, ATMP plants and the push for domestic chip capacity
b: The India Semiconductor Mission is the national programme to build domestic semiconductor manufacturing, assembly, testing, marking and packaging capacity, with approved projects across Gujarat, Assam and Uttar Pradesh and a mix of fabrication, compound semiconductor and ATMP facilities. The strategic logic is straightforward: an AI and search stack that runs on imported accelerators is sovereign at the software layer only. Domestic packaging and eventually fabrication reduce exposure to export controls and supply shocks. For a technology roadmap the realistic reading is that India will build strength in design, packaging and systems integration before leading-edge fabrication, and that system-level innovation, including efficient models and lean inference, is where the near-term advantage lies.

t: India Data and AI Labs: 27 established, 543 more identified, plus 686 AI fellowships
b: Under the IndiaAI Mission's FutureSkills pillar, 27 India Data and AI labs have been established with 543 more identified for expansion, and 686 AI fellowships have been awarded across 178 institutions. The YUVA AI for All programme has seen more than 26.5 lakh individuals complete training, and support extends to over 8,000 undergraduate, 5,000 postgraduate and 500 PhD students. A further 188 additional labs are in progress. The point of the programme is not the headline numbers but the distribution: the labs are placed in institutions outside the handful of metros that already concentrate technology employment, which is what makes a domestic talent pipeline rather than a concentration of it.

t: GIGW and WCAG: the accessibility and quality standards Indian government websites must meet
b: The Guidelines for Indian Government Websites and Apps set mandatory quality requirements for public-facing government digital services, covering usability, accessibility, security, lifecycle management and metadata. They align with the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, which require perceivable, operable, understandable and robust interfaces: text alternatives, keyboard operability, sufficient contrast, resizable text, and compatibility with assistive technology. Government answers in Parliament describe adherence to GIGW and WCAG alongside mobile-first design, multilingual interfaces, AI-powered chatbot support and assisted delivery through Common Service Centres as the standard accessibility package. Any product claiming to serve Indian citizens should treat these as a floor, not a differentiator, and test with a screen reader and at 200 percent zoom.

t: IT Amendment Rules 2026: labelling synthetic content and takedown timelines for deepfakes
b: The Information Technology Rules 2021 and their 2026 amendments provide the baseline intermediary liability structure and enforcement backbone for AI-related harms, including rules on AI-generated and deepfake content with expedited takedown timelines. The India AI Governance Guidelines identify content authentication and provenance as a specific regulatory gap requiring common standards and benchmarks, and recommend embedding transparency, fairness and security by design. For a search engine the operational consequence is that provenance is no longer optional polish: results need an auditable origin, generated summaries need to be marked as generated, and the system should be able to show which source sentence supports which claim. Systems that cannot do this will struggle to comply, and users already distrust answers they cannot trace.

t: CERT-In: incident reporting, vulnerability coordination and national cyber security advisories
b: CERT-In is India's national agency for cyber incident response, coordination and real-time threat advisories, operating under MeitY. Its directions require specified categories of incidents to be reported within defined timelines and require entities to maintain logs for a mandated retention period. Alongside it sit the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre for coordinated cybercrime response, the National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre for strategic sectors, and the National Cyber Coordination Centre for real-time threat monitoring. Government platforms describe compliance with CERT-In and NIC-CERT guidelines, periodic security audits, vulnerability assessment and penetration testing, and continuous monitoring as standard practice. For any product handling user queries at scale, these are the operational baselines for logging, disclosure and incident response.

t: Open Network thinking: why protocol-first beats platform-first for Indian discovery
b: The Beckn protocol, developed as the technical basis for ONDC, separates discovery, ordering and fulfilment into interoperable messages exchanged between participants rather than functions performed inside one application. The consequence is that a buyer app does not need to own inventory, and a seller does not need to be present on every marketplace. India's digital public infrastructure repeats this pattern across identity, payments, documents and language: define a protocol, licence it openly, let many implementations compete. Applied to search, the argument is that a national discovery layer should index and route rather than own and rank behind closed doors, and that the ranking function itself should be inspectable, replaceable and, ideally, locally computed.

t: What a sovereign search engine actually needs: retrieval, language, provenance and compute
b: A search engine is four systems in one. Retrieval turns text into an inverted index and scores documents, classically with BM25 term weighting over title, tags and body fields. Ranking blends lexical score with vector similarity so that paraphrases and Indian language variants still match. Language handling normalises scripts, transliterates roman input and expands synonyms. Provenance attaches an identity to every result so a claim can be traced to a source and a hash. Generation, when added, must be grounded in retrieved passages and must cite them. The full stack can run in a browser with no external service: an inverted index over a few thousand documents, a Merkle tree over document hashes using the platform crypto API, and an extractive answerer that selects source sentences rather than inventing prose.

t: Extractive versus generative answers: why grounded citation beats fluent confidence
b: A generative model asked to summarise retrieval results will sometimes produce a sentence that no retrieved document supports, and the failure is invisible to the reader because the prose is fluent. An extractive answerer has a different failure mode: it can select an irrelevant sentence, but it cannot fabricate one, because every output sentence is quoted from an indexed source with a citation. For high-stakes queries about entitlements, payments or identity, the extractive guarantee is worth more than fluency. The pragmatic architecture is layered: extract first, cite always, and allow a generative model to rewrite only when it is constrained to the retrieved passages and its output is marked as generated. Measure with a citation-support check, not with a fluency judgement.

t: Running an Indian language search layer without a foreign API: the offline-first design
b: The offline-first pattern inverts the usual assumption that search is a service you call. The index, the ranking function and the language normaliser ship with the application; queries never leave the device; the tool works on a train with no signal and on a shared connection where a round trip costs more than the page. For Indian languages the achievable offline layer is smaller but real: script detection, a transliteration table for roman input, a synonym and expansion map for domain terms, and light stemming per script. What cannot be done offline at quality is translation and speech; those belong behind a pluggable adapter that a user can point at Bhashini or a Sarvam endpoint when connectivity and credentials exist, and that degrades to local retrieval when they do not.

t: Speed of light: the universal speed limit and the metre it defines
b: The speed of light in vacuum is exactly 299,792,458 metres per second. Since 1983 this value has been fixed by definition rather than measured, and the metre is defined as the distance light travels in 1/299,792,458 of a second. Light slows in a medium such as glass or water, which is why lenses refract, but the vacuum speed is a constant for every observer. Nothing carrying mass or information can reach it. It sets the ceiling for signal latency on Earth and between planets, and it links space and time in special relativity.

t: Newton's laws of motion and universal gravitation
b: Newton's three laws state that a body stays at rest or in uniform motion unless a force acts; that force equals mass times acceleration; and that every action has an equal and opposite reaction. His law of universal gravitation says every pair of masses attracts with a force proportional to the product of the masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. The framework predicts orbits, tides and projectiles with high accuracy in ordinary conditions, and remains the working model for engineering even though relativity refines it at extreme speeds and masses.

t: Special and general relativity: time dilation and curved spacetime
b: Special relativity holds that the laws of physics are the same for all non-accelerating observers and that the speed of light is constant, so moving clocks run slow and moving lengths contract. General relativity extends this to accelerated frames and treats gravity as the curvature of spacetime produced by mass and energy. The theory predicts gravitational lensing, the precession of Mercury's orbit, black holes and gravitational waves, all since confirmed by observation. It is a practical engineering fact: satellite navigation clocks must be corrected for both special and general relativistic effects or positions drift by kilometres per day.

t: Quantum mechanics: superposition, uncertainty and entanglement
b: Quantum mechanics describes matter at atomic and subatomic scales with a wave function whose square gives the probability of each outcome. A system can exist in a superposition of states until measured, and Heisenberg's uncertainty principle limits how precisely certain paired quantities such as position and momentum can be known together. Entanglement links particles so that their measured properties correlate more strongly than any classical model allows, a resource now used in quantum cryptography, sensing and computing experiments. Quantum effects are not exotic curiosities: they govern chemistry, semiconductors, lasers and the stability of matter itself.

t: The four fundamental forces and the standard model of particles
b: Nature exhibits four fundamental interactions: gravity, electromagnetism, the strong nuclear force that binds quarks into protons and neutrons, and the weak nuclear force responsible for radioactive decay and nuclear fusion in stars. The standard model describes the last three with remarkable precision using quarks, leptons and force-carrying bosons, with the Higgs field explaining particle masses. Gravity is not yet incorporated, which is the central open problem in fundamental physics. The model has been tested to extraordinary accuracy but does not explain dark matter, dark energy or the matter-antimatter asymmetry of the universe.

t: Thermodynamics: energy conservation, entropy and the arrow of time
b: The first law of thermodynamics states that energy cannot be created or destroyed, only converted. The second law says the total entropy of an isolated system never decreases, which is why heat flows from hot to cold, why engines cannot be perfectly efficient and why time appears to have a direction. The third law concerns the approach to absolute zero. Carnot's analysis sets the maximum efficiency of any heat engine from the temperatures of its hot and cold reservoirs, a bound that governs power plants, refrigeration and the thermal design of every data centre and processor.

t: Atoms, the periodic table and the chemical bond
b: Atoms consist of a nucleus of protons and neutrons surrounded by electrons arranged in shells. The periodic table orders elements by atomic number, and position in it predicts chemical behaviour: the alkali metals react vigorously with water, the noble gases are almost inert, and the halogens are aggressive oxidisers. Chemical bonds form by transferring or sharing electrons, giving ionic, covalent and metallic bonding. Molecular shape, determined by electron repulsion, decides properties from the polarity of water to the structure of proteins. Chemistry is the applied study of which bonds break and form under which conditions.

t: Water: the anomalous molecule that makes life and climate possible
b: Water is a bent molecule with strongly polar bonds, so it forms hydrogen bonds with itself and with other substances. Those bonds give it unusual properties: high boiling point for its mass, high heat capacity that moderates climate, high surface tension, and the fact that solid ice is less dense than liquid water, so ice floats and lakes freeze from the top rather than the bottom. Water is an excellent solvent for salts and polar molecules, which is why the chemistry of life happens in it. Its phase changes move enormous quantities of heat through the atmosphere and oceans.

t: DNA, the genetic code and how heredity works
b: DNA is a double helix of two strands linked by base pairs: adenine with thymine, guanine with cytosine. The sequence of bases encodes genes, which are read in triplets called codons and translated into the amino acid chains that fold into proteins. The code is nearly universal across life, from bacteria to humans. Human genomes contain roughly three billion base pairs and about twenty thousand protein-coding genes. Modern tools read and write DNA cheaply, which underpins forensic identification, ancestry testing, gene therapy and CRISPR-based editing, and also raises serious questions about consent and heritable modification.

t: Evolution by natural selection and the tree of life
b: Evolution by natural selection holds that individuals vary, that some variation is heritable, and that variants improving survival and reproduction become more common over generations. Over long spans this produces adaptation and new species. Evidence comes from the fossil record, comparative anatomy, biogeography, embryology and, decisively, molecular genetics: relatedness between species can be read directly from genome sequence. Evolution is not a ladder toward complexity but a branching tree, with most lineages extinct. It explains antibiotic resistance, pesticide resistance, viral variants and the design compromises visible in every organism.

t: Cells: the basic unit of life and how they generate energy
b: All known life is cellular. Prokaryotes, the bacteria and archaea, lack a nucleus; eukaryotes, which include plants, fungi and animals, keep their DNA inside a nuclear membrane and contain organelles. Mitochondria generate most cellular energy by oxidising nutrients and pumping protons across a membrane to make ATP, the universal energy currency. Chloroplasts in plants do the reverse, capturing light to fix carbon. Cell membranes are lipid bilayers studded with proteins that control what enters and leaves. Understanding cells is the basis of immunology, cancer biology, pharmacology and biotechnology.

t: The immune system: innate and adaptive defence
b: The immune system has two cooperating arms. Innate immunity responds within hours using barriers, phagocytes and inflammation, recognising broad patterns rather than specific threats. Adaptive immunity takes days but is precise and memorable: B cells produce antibodies against specific antigens, and T cells kill infected cells or coordinate the response. Memory cells persist for decades, which is why some infections confer lifelong protection and why vaccines work. Vaccination presents a harmless fragment or blueprint of a pathogen so that memory forms without disease, and herd immunity then protects those who cannot be immunised.

t: Photosynthesis and the carbon cycle that regulates climate
b: Photosynthesis uses light to convert carbon dioxide and water into sugars, releasing oxygen. On land, forests and grasslands store carbon in wood and soil; in the ocean, phytoplankton perform roughly half of global photosynthesis and form the base of the marine food web. The carbon cycle moves carbon between atmosphere, biosphere, ocean and rock over timescales from hours to millions of years. Burning fossil fuel moves carbon that was stored underground for geological time into the atmosphere in decades, which is why atmospheric carbon dioxide concentration and global mean temperature are rising together.

t: The solar system: eight planets, moons, asteroids and comets
b: The solar system formed about 4.6 billion years ago from a collapsing cloud of gas and dust. The Sun holds 99.8 percent of its mass. Four rocky planets orbit close in: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars. Beyond the asteroid belt lie two gas giants, Jupiter and Saturn, and two ice giants, Uranus and Neptune. Hundreds of moons, dwarf planets, asteroids and comets complete the inventory. Distances are vast: sunlight takes about eight minutes to reach Earth but over four hours to reach Neptune. Almost all known planetary systems have architectures quite unlike ours, which makes ours informative by contrast.

t: The Sun: structure, solar activity and space weather
b: The Sun is a main-sequence star fusing hydrogen into helium in a core at about fifteen million kelvin. Its outer atmosphere, the corona, is hundreds of times hotter than its visible surface, a puzzle still under study. Magnetic activity produces sunspots, flares and coronal mass ejections that hurl plasma into space. When these reach Earth they drive aurorae, disturb radio communication and navigation, and can damage satellites and power grids, which is why space weather forecasting matters. India's Aditya-L1 mission observes the Sun from the L1 Lagrange point, giving continuous, uninterrupted solar viewing.

t: The Moon, tides and lunar exploration
b: The Moon is tidally locked to Earth, so it always shows the same face. Its gravity, combined with the Sun's, raises tides in the oceans that also slow Earth's rotation and drive the Moon slowly outward. The Moon has no atmosphere, so its surface preserves a four-billion-year impact record. Water ice exists in permanently shadowed polar craters, which makes the poles the focus of exploration. India's Chandrayaan-3 landed near the lunar south pole in August 2023, the first mission to do so, and its measurements confirmed sulphur and other elements in the polar regolith.

t: Mars and India's Mars Orbiter Mission
b: Mars is roughly half Earth's diameter with a thin carbon-dioxide atmosphere, polar ice caps and the largest volcano and canyon in the solar system. Evidence of ancient river valleys and lake beds shows liquid water once flowed. India's Mars Orbiter Mission, launched in November 2013 and inserted into Martian orbit in September 2014, made ISRO the first space agency to reach Mars on its first attempt and at a remarkably low cost. It carried cameras and sensors studying the surface, mineralogy, atmosphere and exosphere, and operated for years beyond its designed life.

t: Black holes, neutron stars and gravitational waves
b: When a massive star exhausts its fuel its core collapses, leaving a neutron star or, above roughly three solar masses, a black hole whose gravity is so strong that not even light escapes its event horizon. Black holes announce themselves through the motion of nearby matter and by merging: colliding black holes radiate gravitational waves, ripples in spacetime predicted by general relativity and first detected directly in 2015. Since then dozens of mergers have been recorded. India is a partner in the LIGO network, with a detector planned at Hingoli in Maharashtra to improve sky localisation.

t: Galaxies, the expanding universe and dark matter
b: Galaxies are gravitationally bound systems of stars, gas, dust and dark matter; the observable universe contains hundreds of billions of them, arranged in filaments and clusters around vast voids. Distant galaxies recede faster the further away they are, which implies an expanding universe that began in a hot dense state about 13.8 billion years ago. Rotation curves of galaxies and the growth of large-scale structure require dark matter, which does not emit light and outweighs ordinary matter roughly five to one. Dark energy, inferred from accelerating expansion, remains unexplained.

t: Plate tectonics, earthquakes and volcanoes
b: Earth's rigid outer shell is broken into plates that move a few centimetres a year on the underlying mantle. Where plates diverge, new crust forms at mid-ocean ridges; where they converge, one descends into subduction zones, building mountain ranges and volcanic arcs; where they slide past each other, stress accumulates and releases as earthquakes. The Himalaya exists because the Indian plate collides with Eurasia, which is why the region experiences frequent large earthquakes. Seismic hazard maps, building codes and early-warning networks are the practical response to living on an active planet.

t: The monsoon: how the Indian summer rainfall system works
b: The Indian summer monsoon is a seasonal reversal of winds driven by differential heating between the landmass and the Indian Ocean, modulated by the Himalayas, the Tibetan plateau and the El Nino southern oscillation. It delivers roughly three quarters of India's annual rainfall between June and September and underpins agriculture, reservoir storage, hydropower and groundwater recharge. Onset, strength and breaks are forecast operationally by the India Meteorological Department using numerical models, satellites and ocean observations. Long-range skill remains limited, which is why monsoon forecasting is one of the most consequential and hardest problems in applied meteorology.

t: Climate change: the physical evidence and the carbon budget
b: Atmospheric carbon dioxide concentration has risen from about 280 parts per million before industrialisation to over 420 today, driven mainly by burning coal, oil and gas. Global mean surface temperature has increased by about 1.2 degrees Celsius above the pre-industrial baseline, with most of that warming in the last fifty years. Sea level is rising through thermal expansion and ice loss, oceans are acidifying, and heatwaves, heavy rainfall and drought intensity are shifting. The remaining carbon budget for holding warming near 1.5 degrees is small, which makes every year of emissions decisive.

t: Biodiversity, ecosystems and the sixth extinction
b: Biodiversity is the variety of genes, species and ecosystems. It supplies food, medicine, pollination, water purification and climate regulation, and its loss is not reversible on human timescales. The main drivers are habitat conversion, overexploitation, pollution, invasive species and climate change. Current extinction rates are far above the background rate in the fossil record, which is why the episode is called the sixth mass extinction. India is one of the world's megadiverse countries, holding roughly eight percent of recorded species within about two and a half percent of global land area, and its protected areas and tiger reserves are central to conservation.

t: The transistor, integrated circuits and Moore's law
b: A transistor is a switch made of semiconductor material whose conductivity is controlled by an electric field, voltage or current. Replacing vacuum tubes with transistors in the 1950s made electronics small, cheap and reliable. Integrating many transistors on one chip gave the microprocessor, and the observation that transistor counts doubled roughly every two years became known as Moore's law, an economic roadmap rather than a law of physics. That pace has slowed as features approach atomic dimensions, pushing the industry toward new architectures, chiplets, three-dimensional stacking and specialised accelerators.

t: How the internet works: packets, TCP/IP and the domain name system
b: The internet is a network of networks that moves data in packets. Internet Protocol addresses each device and routes packets hop by hop; Transmission Control Protocol orders them, detects loss and retransmits, providing a reliable stream on an unreliable network. The domain name system translates human-readable names into addresses through a distributed hierarchy of resolvers and authoritative servers. Border gateway protocol lets autonomous networks advertise routes to each other. Together these simple, open, layered protocols allow any device to talk to any other without central permission, which is the property that made the network grow.

t: The World Wide Web, browsers and how search engines index the web
b: The web is an application on top of the internet: documents identified by URLs, transferred by HTTP and written in HTML, linked by hyperlinks. A search engine works in three stages. Crawlers fetch pages by following links. Indexers parse the text and build an inverted index mapping each word to the documents containing it, alongside signals such as link structure and freshness. At query time a ranking function scores documents for relevance, blending lexical match, popularity and personalisation. The whole system depends on crawl budgets, robots directives and the willingness of publishers to be indexed.

t: Public key cryptography and how HTTPS protects a connection
b: Public key cryptography uses a pair of mathematically linked keys: what one encrypts, only the other can decrypt. It solves key distribution, because the public key can be published. In practice a TLS handshake uses asymmetric cryptography to authenticate the server via a certificate and to agree a shared secret, then switches to fast symmetric encryption such as AES for the session. Hash functions provide integrity and are the basis of digital signatures and blockchain ledgers. Security depends as much on key management, certificate authorities and implementation discipline as on the algorithms themselves.

t: Machine learning, neural networks and deep learning
b: Machine learning fits models to data rather than encoding rules by hand. A neural network stacks layers of weighted sums and nonlinear activations; training adjusts the weights by gradient descent to reduce a loss function on examples. Deep networks with many layers learn hierarchies of features, which made breakthroughs in vision, speech and language possible once data and compute were sufficient. Key practical concerns are generalisation to unseen data, distribution shift, bias inherited from training data, interpretability, and the cost of training and serving large models, which is why efficient architectures and local inference matter.

t: Transformers and large language models: attention, tokens and context
b: A transformer processes text as tokens and uses self-attention to weigh every token against every other, which lets it capture long-range dependencies without recurrent state. Large language models stack many such blocks, pretrain on trillions of tokens to predict the next token, then post-train with instruction data and human or model feedback. Capability scales with parameters, data and compute, though with diminishing returns and rising cost. Mixture-of-experts designs activate only part of the network per token, cutting inference cost. Known failure modes include confident fabrication, stale knowledge, prompt sensitivity and weak arithmetic without tool use.

t: Retrieval-augmented generation and why citation matters
b: Retrieval-augmented generation pairs a search step with a language model: relevant passages are retrieved first, then supplied to the model, which answers using them. This grounds the output in citable material and lets knowledge be updated by re-indexing rather than retraining. It also constrains the model to a corpus, which reduces fabrication but does not eliminate it, because the model can still misread or overstate what the passage says. The reliable pattern is to show the passage alongside the claim, attach an identifier, and let the reader verify the source directly rather than trusting a summary.

t: BM25 and the mathematics of keyword search ranking
b: BM25 scores a document for a query by summing, over query terms, a term-frequency component damped by document length and weighted by inverse document frequency. Two parameters control behaviour: k1 sets how quickly repeated occurrences stop adding value, and b sets how strongly long documents are penalised. Inverse document frequency makes rare words decisive and common words nearly worthless. BM25 is decades old and still competitive with dense retrieval on many tasks, which is why production systems often combine the two: lexical matching for precision on names and numbers, vector similarity for paraphrase.

t: Vector embeddings and approximate nearest neighbour search
b: An embedding maps text to a vector so that semantically similar content lands nearby. Retrieval then becomes nearest-neighbour search, usually by cosine similarity. Exact search over millions of vectors is too slow, so systems use approximate indexes such as HNSW graphs or product quantisation, trading a little recall for large speed gains. Embeddings generalise across wording but are weak on exact identifiers, negation and numbers, so hybrid scoring with lexical retrieval is standard practice. Their quality depends entirely on the model that produced them and the domain it was trained on.

t: Cryptographic hashing, Merkle trees and tamper evidence
b: A cryptographic hash maps any input to a fixed-length output such that small input changes produce unpredictable output changes, and finding two inputs with the same output is infeasible. SHA-256 produces 256 bits. A Merkle tree hashes leaves and then hashes pairs of hashes upward to a single root. Publishing only the root commits to the entire dataset, and any single item can later be proven to belong by supplying the handful of sibling hashes on its path. Verification costs logarithmic work instead of re-reading everything, which is why Merkle trees underpin certificate transparency, version control and blockchain ledgers.

t: Blockchain: distributed ledgers, consensus and the permissioned distinction
b: A blockchain is an append-only ledger of hash-linked blocks replicated across participants. Consensus rules decide which block is next: proof of work spends energy, proof of stake bonds capital, and permissioned networks use voting or ordering services among known validators. Smart contracts are programs executed deterministically by every node, so their results are agreed without a trusted intermediary. Permissioned networks trade openness for throughput, privacy and known identity, which suits government record keeping. The honest limitation is that a ledger guarantees integrity of what was written, not truth of what was written.

t: Quantum computing: qubits, gates and where the advantage lies
b: A qubit stores a superposition of zero and one, and entangled qubits share correlations that classical bits cannot reproduce. Quantum algorithms exploit interference to concentrate probability on correct answers: Shor's algorithm factors integers exponentially faster than known classical methods, and Grover's gives a quadratic speedup for unstructured search. Real machines are noisy, so error correction requires many physical qubits per logical one. Near-term value is expected first in simulating molecules and materials rather than breaking cryptography. India has a national quantum mission building computing, communication, sensing and metrology capabilities.

t: Semiconductors: how chips are fabricated and why fabs matter
b: Chips are built layer by layer on silicon wafers using photolithography to pattern circuits, then doping, deposition and etching to create transistors and interconnects. Advanced nodes require extreme ultraviolet lithography and operate at dimensions of a few nanometres, where quantum tunnelling and heat become dominant constraints. A fabrication plant costs billions and needs ultra-pure water, gases and stable power, which is why the industry is concentrated in a few regions. Packaging and testing are a lower-capital entry point, and India's semiconductor mission is building capacity in exactly those stages first.

t: Solar photovoltaics: from photons to grid parity
b: A photovoltaic cell absorbs light, frees electrons in a semiconductor junction and drives them through an external circuit. Most commercial modules use crystalline silicon; thin-film and perovskite technologies offer lower cost or higher efficiency per weight, and perovskite-silicon tandems have pushed laboratory efficiencies well above single-junction limits. Module prices have fallen more than ninety percent in a decade, making solar the cheapest new electricity in many markets. The binding constraints have shifted from cost to land, grid capacity, storage and the variability of output across the day and the season.

t: Batteries, energy storage and the electrification of transport
b: Lithium-ion batteries move lithium ions between electrodes during charge and discharge. Energy density has roughly tripled since commercialisation and cost has fallen by an order of magnitude, which is what made electric vehicles and grid storage viable. Chemistry choices trade energy density against safety, cycle life and the availability of materials: lithium iron phosphate is cheaper and safer but heavier per unit energy, while nickel-rich cells store more in less mass. Sodium-ion and flow batteries are emerging for stationary storage. Recycling, mineral supply and charging infrastructure are the practical bottlenecks.

t: Nuclear fission, fusion and the future of baseload power
b: Fission splits heavy nuclei such as uranium-235, releasing energy from mass difference and sustaining a chain reaction moderated and controlled in a reactor. It provides steady low-carbon baseload but produces long-lived radioactive waste and requires rigorous safety culture. India operates a fleet of pressurised heavy water reactors and is building a thorium programme around its large monazite reserves. Fusion instead combines light nuclei, as the Sun does; it produces far less long-lived waste but requires confining plasma at over a hundred million kelvin, and net energy gain remains an engineering challenge rather than a solved problem.

t: Grids, transmission and why electricity storage decides renewable share
b: An electricity grid must balance generation and demand instantaneously, because storage on the grid is still small relative to daily consumption. Frequency and voltage are the control signals: too little generation and frequency falls. Transmission capacity determines whether cheap generation in one region can reach demand in another, which is why interconnectors and long-distance high-voltage direct current lines matter. Renewables shift the problem from fuel to flexibility: storage, demand response, flexible hydro and gas peaking, and better forecasting. India's national grid is one of the largest synchronised networks in the world, integrating regional systems into a single frequency pool.

t: Water supply, sanitation and the global burden of waterborne disease
b: Safe water, sanitation and hygiene are the most cost-effective public health interventions known. Contaminated water transmits cholera, typhoid, dysentery and hepatitis A, and poor sanitation drives soil-transmitted helminths and stunting through repeated childhood infection. Treatment combines source protection, filtration, chlorination and safe storage; sanitation requires containment, conveyance and treatment rather than latrines alone. Behaviour change and reliable operation matter as much as construction, which is why infrastructure without maintenance fails. India's Jal Jeevan Mission has extended piped household water connections at large scale, with water quality testing as the persistent challenge.

t: Vaccination programmes and the eradication of smallpox
b: Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980 after a global campaign combining mass vaccination with ring vaccination around each case. It remains the only human disease eradicated, and the template has been applied to polio, which is now close to elimination with only a few countries reporting cases. Routine immunisation against measles, diphtheria, pertussis, tetanus, hepatitis B and others prevents millions of deaths each year. Success depends on cold chain integrity, supply, trust and coverage: outbreaks reappear where coverage falls below the herd immunity threshold, and vaccine hesitancy is now a first-order public health risk.

t: Tuberculosis, antimicrobial resistance and the long war against infection
b: Tuberculosis is caused by a bacterium spread through the air, and it remains among the leading infectious causes of death worldwide, with India carrying the largest share of cases. Treatment requires a multi-drug course over months, and incomplete courses breed resistance. Antimicrobial resistance arises whenever bacteria are exposed to drugs long enough to select resistant variants, driven by overuse in human medicine and livestock and by poor infection control. Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis needs longer, more toxic and far costlier regimens. Stewardship, rapid diagnostics, adherence support and new drug classes are the available levers.

t: Non-communicable disease: diabetes, hypertension and the epidemiological shift
b: Non-communicable diseases now cause the majority of deaths worldwide, and in India they dominate the burden in every state. Diabetes arises when insulin action or secretion fails, damaging blood vessels and nerves over years; hypertension silently raises the risk of stroke, heart attack and kidney failure. Both are strongly associated with diet, physical activity, tobacco and alcohol, and both are largely manageable when detected early and treated consistently. The hard problems are screening at population scale, adherence to lifelong medication, and the cost of care, which pushes families into debt.

t: Mental health: the treatment gap and what works
b: Depression and anxiety disorders are among the largest contributors to years lived with disability, and the majority of people affected worldwide receive no treatment at all. Effective interventions exist: psychological therapies such as cognitive behavioural therapy, antidepressant medication for moderate and severe cases, and community-based care delivered by trained non-specialists. Stigma, distance, cost and a severe shortage of psychiatrists and clinical psychologists keep the treatment gap wide. Digital and telephone-delivered care extends reach, but must be paired with clear escalation pathways and protection of privacy, since mental health data is unusually sensitive.

t: Nutrition: macronutrients, micronutrients and the double burden
b: Human nutrition requires energy and protein for growth and maintenance, essential fatty acids, and micronutrients such as iron, iodine, zinc, vitamin A, folate and vitamin B12. Deficiencies cause anaemia, impaired cognition, stunting and weakened immunity; excess energy intake causes obesity and metabolic disease. Many countries, including India, face both at once: undernutrition persists in some groups while obesity and diabetes rise in others. Fortification, supplementation, dietary diversity, and improving the quality rather than only the quantity of food are the practical policy instruments.

t: Epidemiology: incidence, prevalence, relative risk and study design
b: Incidence counts new cases in a period; prevalence counts all existing cases at a point. Relative risk compares outcome rates between exposed and unexposed groups; attributable risk estimates how much disease would disappear if exposure were removed. Study designs trade rigour for feasibility: randomised controlled trials support causal claims, cohort studies follow exposure forward, case-control studies look backward from outcome, and cross-sectional surveys describe a moment. Bias, confounding and measurement error are the recurring threats, and no statistical technique fully repairs a badly designed study.

t: Antibiotics: discovery, mechanism and the resistance clock
b: Antibiotics kill bacteria or stop them multiplying by attacking structures absent in human cells: cell walls, bacterial ribosomes, DNA replication enzymes or folate synthesis. Penicillin's discovery in 1928 opened the antibiotic era and added roughly two decades to average life expectancy. Every antibiotic class has eventually met resistance, and the pipeline of genuinely new classes is thin because development is scientifically hard and commercially unattractive. Responsible use means prescribing only when bacterial infection is likely, completing courses appropriately, and controlling use in agriculture where most tonnage is consumed.

t: The scientific method, peer review and reproducibility
b: The scientific method is a disciplined loop: observe, form a testable hypothesis, predict, test, and revise. Its authority comes from falsifiability and replication rather than from authority of persons.
